extracted.intended_audience: activists, legal researchers, journalists and the public interested in the legal history of the Bhopal disaster
extracted.subtask_description: A chronological summary of the criminal proceedings and related legal/procedural developments against Union Carbide and associated persons/corporations arising from the 1984 Bhopal gas disaster. Covers charges, court orders, jurisdictional disputes, settlement effects, extradition issues, and service of process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder (IPC section 304)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian Penal Code, section 304, ch. 16. Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Whoever commits culpable homicide not amounting to murder shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine... or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, or with fine, or with both, if the act is done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death, but without any intention to cause death..." (verbatim excerpt provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification as non-bailable offence
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain charges were described as 'non-bailable' affecting arrest and bail procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from timeline: Warren Anderson was arrested on a charge described as 'non-bailable' yet released on bail; classification as non-bailable ordinarily makes bail not a matter of right and affects arrest/release procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quashing of criminal proceedings to effectuate civil settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court ordered that 'To enable the effectuation of the settlement… all criminal proceedings related to and arising out of the disaster shall stand quashed wherever these may be pending.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court power to quash criminal proceedings as part of or to implement a civil settlement; this can extinguish parallel criminal actions across forums unless later revoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court revocation of immunity and remedial orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court later revoked criminal immunity granted to UCC and all accused and ordered remedial measures (e.g., construction of a 500-bed hospital with costs borne by UCC and UCIL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts can both revive criminal proceedings and impose remedial or injunctive measures on corporations as part of judgments; such orders may coexist with civil settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution/diution of charges (culpable homicide to negligence - section 304A)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1996 the appeal quashed culpable homicide charges against the Indian accused and directed they be charged under section 304-A (causing death by negligence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutorial or judicial re-characterisation of charges can reduce severity (from intentional or knowledge-based homicide to negligence), with implications for punishment and extradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extradition treaty requirements (Indo-US Articles 2(1) and 9(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 2: 'An offense shall be an extraditable offense if it is punishable under the laws in both Contracting States by deprivation of liberty including imprisonment, for a period of more than one year or by a more severe penalty.' Article 9(3): requires 'such information as would justify the committal for trial of the person if the offense had been committed in the Requested State.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extradition requests must meet dual criminality and evidentiary/committal-information thresholds; failure to satisfy these may lead to refusal (as occurred with the US refusal of India's request for Warren Anderson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-extraditable offence determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain offences (e.g., criminal negligence as characterised by domestic actors) may be non-extraditable under treaty terms or as interpreted by the requested state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeline example: CBI's application to dilute main charge against Anderson from culpable homicide to criminal negligence (a non-extraditable offence) was opposed; the US State Department later refused extradition citing treaty requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of separate legal personality and forum non conveniens defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Union Carbide invoked the doctrine of separate legal personality and argued the US was an improper forum: 'The Bhopal plant was managed, operated and maintained entirely by Indians in India.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate defendants may assert separate corporate personality and forum non conveniens to resist foreign jurisdiction; courts examine locus of conduct, control, and corporate linkages when assessing jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to attach shares and properties to secure appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities attached the shares and properties of Union Carbide India (UCIL) to ensure appearance in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asset attachment/attachment orders are an enforcement tool to secure defendants' or corporations' presence in proceedings where personal jurisdiction or service is contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuing, serving, and non-service of summons and warrants; declaration of absconding
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple summons issued against Anderson and UCC were not served; warrants were issued and, upon non-appearance, individuals/entities were declared 'absconding'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper service is prerequisite to in-person process; failure to serve can lead to non-appearance designations, which may trigger further measures (warrants, attachment, ex parte actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT) limitations in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite the US being signatory to a Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty on Criminal Matters with India, DOJ did not serve notices on Dow when Indian courts attempted service via US authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MLAT channels exist for cross-border service and evidence requests but can fail in practice due to executive decisions or treaty-processing constraints, limiting enforcement of foreign criminal summons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court power to issue summons to successor/parent corporations and to consider 'show cause' applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Bhopal CJM ordered summons be issued to Dow (UCC's successor) to 'show cause' why it did not produce UCC before the Bhopal court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may attempt to bring parent or successor corporations before them by issuing show-cause notices; corporate restructuring and share transfers complicate enforcement and may be contested in higher courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural stay and high court intervention on service/summons
rubrics_metrics.description: High Court granted stay on summons against Dow after DCIPL filed an appeal seeking to quash the CJM order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher courts can grant interim relief (stay) against lower court orders on summons/service, which can impede or delay enforcement of trial-court process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to serve notices electronically and modern service methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A new procedure allows the Bhopal courts to serve notices by electronic means; since January 2017, multiple summons have been served directly on Ms. Amy Wilson, Corporate Secretary and Associate General Counsel of Dow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic service is an evolving procedural option to reach foreign entities or representatives; courts may adopt such methods when traditional service via foreign authorities fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeding ex parte for wilful violation of summons
rubrics_metrics.description: An application was filed urging the CJM to proceed ex parte under earlier orders against the Dow Chemical Company for wilful violation of summons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a party wilfully ignores process, courts may be moved to proceed ex parte (in absence) and seek remedies or sanctions; this is an enforcement mechanism when service and attendance fail.
